title: Coins (1p or 2p) and a written safety guide: wash hands after, no coins near mouths
subject: Art & Design
unit: Spring 2: Still life and a paper bridge (Still Life and Can You Make a Paper Bridge?)
source: Written for art/y2 lesson 7 (Coins (1p or 2p) and a written safety guide: wash hands after, no coins near mouths)
intro: Lesson 7: Can you make a paper bridge? (DT). Listen, look, then do the tasks with a grown-up.

parts.text: Add one coin at a time

blocks.h: Safety guide: testing paper bridges with coins

practical.aim: To find out which paper bridge shape holds the most coins
equipment: Two books the same height, about 15 cm apart
safety: Wash your hands after handling coins
Keep coins away from mouths (and away from little brothers and sisters)
An adult knows what you are doing and is nearby
method: Lay a flat sheet of paper across the gap between the books
Put coins in the middle one at a time until it falls; count them
Fold a new sheet into a zigzag (concertina) and test it the same way
Roll or fold a third sheet into a new shape and test it
Do each test twice and record the numbers in the table

keywords.def: does not break or bend easily

questions.q: Predict: which will hold more coins, flat or zigzag?
Core: Test a flat and a zigzag bridge. Record the coins in the table.
questions.a: For example: flat 0 or 1 coin; zigzag several coins

questions.q: Extend: Try a rolled tube bridge.
questions.a: A result recorded for the tube

questions.q: Stretch: Say why the folds help.
questions.a: The folds make the paper stiff, so it does not bend under the coins

questions.q: To make it a fair test we keep the same:
questions.a: A) Gap. We keep the gap and paper size the same and change only the bridge shape.

questions.q: Which bridge held more coins in most tests?
Big question: how can one sheet of paper hold up coins?
questions.a: Fold it into zigzags or tubes so it is stiff and strong
